L131: ##### Evaluation Integrity
L132: As discussed in Section cite7†2 , monorepo infrastructure constraints can prevent reproducing the exact environment at a past commit. However, hiding the solution diff from the agent’s environment helps ensure the agent does not “cheat” on a task by reading the committed solution files. We achieve this by backing out the solution diff from the current repository and running the agent evaluation on top of the backed out commit.
L179: We present evaluation results across three dimensions: model performance comparison, harness evaluation, and qualitative analysis. We run the evaluation on the F2P subset of the benchmark, i.e., only on diffs that have at least one fail-to-pass test.
L180: ### 4.1 Model Evaluation
L181: We evaluated multiple large language models on ProdCodeBench using the strong diff partition. Each model was evaluated three times to measure variance. Figure cite53†3 (left) presents the solve rates with 95% confidence intervals. The evaluation results reveal clear performance tiers among the models. Claude Opus achieves the highest solve rate, followed by Claude Sonnet. This suggests that models from the same family scale predictably with capability—Opus outperforms Sonnet, which in turn outperforms Haiku.
L183: ### 4.2 Harness Evaluation
L184: We compare two evaluation harnesses on ProdCodeBench. Agent-Basic uses a more limited toolset and simpler search tools. Agent-IDE features a comprehensive toolset with prompts designed to generalize across both GPT and Claude series models. The Agent-IDE harness has roughly 3x more tools than Agent-Basic, reflecting a full IDE-like experience: code navigation, local diagnostics, formatting, and knowledge search.

L89: To address these limitations, we propose ByteRover, an agent-native memory architecture that inverts the relationship between agent and memory. Instead of calling an external memory service, the same LLM that reasons about a task also curates knowledge into a hierarchical Context Tree—a file-based knowledge graph where each entry carries explicit relations, provenance, and lifecycle metadata.

L317: A fundamental discrepancy exists between the operational logic of HMO and the evaluation protocols of current benchmarks like LoCoMo and LongMemEval. These datasets typically adopt a decoupled evaluation paradigm where the interaction history is provided as a static corpus and questions are treated as isolated retrieval tasks. This structure fails to account for the temporal coherence and iterative evolution that characterize how users and agents engage in the real world.
L320: To bridge this gap, we will continue to investigate whether more robust benchmarks exist that rely on interaction and can effectively simulate this co-evolutionary process. The current lack of standardized evaluation suites that measure how an agent prepares its internal memory structure for future and coherent follow-ups remains a significant challenge. Consequently, we aim to further explore the potential for proposing a novel evaluation framework centered on the user.

L62: To address these limitations, we introduce ATBench, a trajectory-level benchmark that enables structured, diverse, and realistic evaluation of agent safety. ATBench formulates agentic safety risks along three orthogonal dimensions—risk source, failure mode, and real-world harm—providing a controllable framework for capturing diverse risk patterns.
L70: Despite this shift, existing agent safety benchmarks remain limited in their ability to capture trajectory-level risks. Specifically, they suffer from three key limitations. First, they provide insufficient interaction diversity, relying on restricted tool ecosystems and narrow scenario coverage that fail to reflect real-world agent deployments.
L71: Second, they offer limited observability of safety failures, where coarse-grained labels obscure the underlying causes, behaviors, and consequences of unsafe outcomes. Third, they are lack of long-horizon realism, as short or simplified trajectories fail to capture delayed, context-dependent risk emergence. These limitations are reflected across existing trajectory-level benchmarks cite43†Yuan et al. (2024a) ; cite44†Luo et al. (2025) , as summarized in Table cite47†1 .
L72: To address these limitations, we introduce ATBench, a trajectory-level benchmark designed around a simple objective: maximize diversity while preserving realism under long-horizon interactions. In this paper, we organize agent safety along three orthogonal dimensions—risk source, failure mode, and real-world harm—and use this taxonomy together with a heterogeneous tool ecosystem to support controllable and diverse benchmark construction.
L73: We further incorporate a delayed-trigger long-context protocol so that risks can be planted early, realized later, and evaluated under realistic multi-step interaction. The current release contains 1,000 held-out trajectories (503 safe and 497 unsafe), with 2,084 available tools, 1,954 invoked tools, and an average of 9.01 turns per trajectory. To improve reliability, we apply post-generation filtering followed by a five-reviewer full human audit.
L194: Limitations. ATBench still has limitations. First, each unsafe trajectory carries only one primary label per taxonomy dimension, which may miss valid secondary interpretations in multi-causal cases. Second, all trajectories are constructed in English; extending the benchmark to multilingual settings would broaden its applicability to global agent deployments. Third, the benchmark focuses on text-and-tool trajectories; multimodal and embodied settings remain important future extensions.
